about.author: Zyphullen
about.certainty_rule: green = established (known science, or a defined / proved result in Maths); orange = leading idea / partial progress; red = unknown / open problem. A link takes the colour of its less-certain end.

suggest_a_fix.subject: Echo Atlas fix: <Card name> (<card id>)
suggest_a_fix.note: Every card has a Suggest a fix button that opens a prefilled e-mail (section, card, card id, version, page link). Card ids: fntu/<id>, maths/<id>, history/<id>-<n>, cell/<id>, body/<id>, planet/<id>, element/<symbol>, <section>/link/<from>><to>.

about.what_this_file_holds: A dated timeline (one or more landmarks for every Maths node), across five eras. Proposed ideas are kept apart from proofs.
about.how_to_use: Every item has id, title, certainty, summary, details and sources (title, url, type). Full source details (year, link check) are in sources_used. A link's reason_sources are the sources on its two cards. Fact-check against the sources; flag anything that looks wrong or out of date.

maths_history.note: A selected dated landmark for every map node. A publication date is not always an invention or discovery date. Broad subjects retain a landmark or approximate range; the chart does not measure completeness or certify priority between simultaneous contributors.
maths_history.scale: Non-linear proportional time within eras; cumulative selected publication/proposal milestones, not completeness

events.label: c. 20,000 BCE
events.text: Ishango bone: an approximate, debated record associated with early counting — not a claimed first mathematical act.

sources.title: Ishango bone — historical overview and alternative interpretations

events.label: c. 1800 BCE
events.text: Old Babylonian place-value systems are a documented landmark. Indian and other decimal traditions are not collapsed into this one date.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.label: c. 300 BCE
events.text: Euclid’s Elements — an approximate traditional date, not a certificate that all its ideas originated with Euclid.

events.label: c. 300 BCE
events.text: Euclid’s proof that there are infinitely many primes is a classical anchor for prime-number mathematics.
Brahmagupta gives arithmetic rules for zero as a number.

events.label: c. 820
events.text: Al-Khwarizmi’s algebra treatise; the date is approximate. Algebra has multiple textual traditions and later developments.
Grassmann’s Ausdehnungslehre is a landmark in the development of vector-space ideas, not the invention of every vector notion.
Cayley publishes A Memoir on the Theory of Matrices.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

events.text: Cayley’s matrix memoir includes the characteristic-equation result named for Cayley and Hamilton.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

events.text: Hilbert’s integral-equation papers are a dated landmark in Hilbert-space methods; physical interpretation comes from later quantum mechanics.

sources.title: MIT OpenCourseWare: Quantum Theory I — mathematical formalism

events.label: c. 300 BCE
events.text: Euclid’s Elements becomes a durable model of deductive proof. Logical inquiry already had many cultural and historical roots.
Zermelo’s axiomatisation (1908); Fraenkel and Skolem’s contributions (1922) lead to ZFC.

sources.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: set theory

events.text: Turing and Church formalise computability independently in the 1930s.

events.label: c. 300 BCE
events.text: Euclid’s algorithm for greatest common divisors supplies the landmark; the later word “algorithm” has a separate etymology.
Gödel’s incompleteness theorem is published.
Cantor’s first set-theory paper establishes a landmark in the theory of infinite sets.
Cantor’s diagonal argument is presented and appears in a volume dated 1890–91, later printed. The range preserves that bibliographic nuance.

sources.title: Cantor’s diagonal argument — original text and translation

events.text: Wallis presents a geometric representation of complex numbers. A landmark, not the final modern theory.

sources.title: MacTutor: the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and complex numbers

events.text: Gauss’s Disquisitiones gives a systematic treatment of congruences and arithmetic residues.
Alphonse de Polignac publishes a more general prime-gap conjecture that includes infinitely many prime pairs differing by two.

sources.title: Polignac’s conjecture (1849): overview and original reference

events.text: Christian Goldbach and Leonhard Euler’s correspondence gives the statement now associated with Goldbach’s name.

events.label: c. 1937 · first journal record traced to 1971
events.text: The Collatz problem circulated in the twentieth century and is often dated to 1937; the first journal appearance is later. The date is not presented as exact.

sources.title: Lagarias: The 3x+1 problem and its generalizations (1985)

events.text: Fermat records his famous assertion in the margin.

sources.title: Wiles: Modular elliptic curves and Fermat’s Last Theorem (1995)

events.text: Andrew Wiles and Richard Taylor publish the corrected proof. The 1993 announcement and 1994 correction are separate milestones.

sources.title: Wiles: Modular elliptic curves and Fermat’s Last Theorem (1995)
Taylor & Wiles: Ring-theoretic properties of Hecke algebras (1995)

events.label: c. 1800 BCE · selected tradition
events.text: Ancient mathematical traditions used right-triangle relationships. This is not a claimed discovery year assigned to Pythagoras.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.text: Descartes publishes La Géométrie; Fermat’s related work circulated in the same period.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.label: c. 5th century BCE → medieval astronomy
events.text: Trigonometry developed through Greek, Indian, Islamic and other astronomical traditions. No single inventor/date is assigned.
Lobachevsky publishes non-Euclidean geometry in 1829; Bolyai follows in 1832.

events.label: 19th–20th century · selected landmark: modern arithmetic geometry
events.text: Elliptic-curve arithmetic has many historical layers; this range marks their modern development without crediting all of them to one person.

events.label: 1825–1828 survey; 1854 Riemann follows
events.text: Gauss’s investigations of curved surfaces are a landmark. Riemann’s 1854 geometry lecture is a separate anchor.

sources.title: Gauss: General Investigations of Curved Surfaces — translation with original context

events.text: Johannes Kepler proposes the sphere-packing conjecture.

sources.title: Hales: A proof of the Kepler conjecture (Annals, 2005)

events.label: 1998 announced · 2005–2006 publication
events.text: The proof announcement and its formal publication are separated. Flyspeck completed a formal proof later.

sources.title: Hales: A proof of the Kepler conjecture (Annals, 2005)
Hales et al.: A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture (2017)

events.text: Francis Guthrie poses the four-colour question.
Appel and Haken publish the computer-assisted proof. The original paper appeared in 1977; later formal verification is a separate milestone.

sources.title: Appel & Haken: Every planar map is four colorable, Part I (1977)

events.text: Henri Poincaré poses the conjecture in his fifth complement to Analysis Situs.
Grigori Perelman announces the proof in preprints posted in 2002 and 2003.
Poincaré’s Analysis Situs is a foundational landmark in algebraic topology.
Poincaré’s fundamental-group and topology work is a landmark; higher homotopy theory developed later.
Tait’s On Knots is the map’s dated knot-table landmark, not a claim that knots had never been studied before.
Riemann’s geometry lecture is the historical anchor for the card.
Eilenberg and Mac Lane publish General Theory of Natural Equivalences.

sources.title: Mac Lane: Categories for the Working Mathematician (Springer)

events.label: 1832 · manuscript; 1846 published
events.text: Galois leaves his group-theoretic ideas in a manuscript in 1832; Liouville publishes Galois’s work in 1846.
Lie-group and representation theory are treated as parts of a broader development, not as simultaneous discoveries.

events.label: 1950 · proceedings published 1952
events.text: W. V. D. Hodge presents the conjecture at the International Congress of Mathematicians; its proceedings appear later.
Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer develop and publish the conjecture as a range of work, not a single-day announcement.
Fermat and Pascal’s correspondence on the problem of points is a landmark in probability theory.
Thomas Bayes’s essay is published posthumously by Richard Price.

sources.title: Bayes and Price (1763) — Royal Society original

events.text: Shannon’s information-entropy formalism is published, with its thermodynamic context acknowledged in the card.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

events.text: Kolmogorov’s axioms are one dated formal anchor for randomness; philosophical and algorithmic definitions have other histories.

sources.title: Kolmogorov: Foundations of the Theory of Probability (English translation)
Kolmogorov: Foundations of the Theory of Probability (English translation)

events.text: Cauchy’s approach to rigorous limits is a historical progression, culminating here in the 1821 Cours d’analyse.
Cauchy’s Cours d’analyse is a landmark in rigorous convergence and series theory.

events.label: early 19th century · 1807/1822
events.text: Fourier’s work on heat developed through a memoir and later 1822 publication. The range makes the chronology explicit.
Riemann’s geometry lecture supplies the map’s historical anchor for manifold ideas.
Dedekind publishes a rigorous construction of real numbers using cuts.

sources.title: Dedekind (1872) — continuity and irrational numbers (in Essays on the Theory of Numbers, Project Gutenberg)
MacTutor: the real numbers and their history

events.text: Numerical analysis is a broad development, not a single dated invention.
Navier and Stokes contribute to the equations; these are publication dates.
Clay formulates the existence-and-smoothness prize problem. Later claimed work must not be treated as accepted resolution.
Yang and Mills publish their equations.
Clay formulates the rigorous quantum Yang–Mills existence and mass-gap prize problem.
Euler’s zeta product, Dirichlet’s 1837 L-functions, and Riemann’s 1859 paper are separate landmarks for this broad node.

sources.title: A history of L-functions — LMFDB, reviewed

events.text: Bernhard Riemann publishes the hypothesis about the nontrivial zeros of the zeta function.
Cook’s theorem gives a precise anchor for the P versus NP problem; independent Soviet work also matters.

sources.title: P versus NP problem — Clay Mathematics Institute

events.label: 1654 · Pascal–Fermat correspondence; broader combinatorics older
events.text: This paper’s selected combinatorics anchor is the Pascal–Fermat problem-of-points correspondence. Discrete enumeration itself has older traditions.
Frank Ramsey publishes On a Problem of Formal Logic.

sources.title: Ramsey: On a Problem of Formal Logic (1930; Oxford Academic)

events.label: c. 300 BCE · Euclid; Gauss 1801 · modern number theory
events.text: Euclid provides an ancient landmark; Gauss’s 1801 Disquisitiones is a separate modern systematic landmark.

events.label: 16th–17th-century notation · arithmetic older
events.text: This node uses an approximate symbolic-notation range, not an invention date for arithmetic itself.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.label: c. 1800 BCE · ancient fractions
events.text: Ancient arithmetic records include fractions and ratios. The modern number concept evolved across cultures.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.text: Grassmann’s extension theory is a landmark for abstract vector-space ideas, not their only possible origin.

sources.title: Axler: Linear Algebra Done Right, fourth edition (free author copy)

events.text: The Hilbert-school work supplies a landmark for infinite-dimensional inner-product methods; finite-dimensional geometry is older.
Leibniz’s term “function” is a notation/concept landmark. Functions evolved beyond that early use.

sources.title: MacTutor: an overview of the history of mathematics

events.text: Cardano publishes Ars Magna, including cubic and quartic solution methods, amid a long older history of polynomial problems.
Frege publishes Begriffsschrift. Aristotle is not replaced as a historical root by this publication milestone.

sources.title: Frege, Gottlob and the Formula Language of Pure Thinking — MacTutor
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: classical logic

events.text: Pearson’s chi-squared goodness-of-fit paper is a landmark for this node, not a claimed origin of all statistics.
Shannon’s information theory establishes limits for compression and communication.

sources.title: Shannon: A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948)

events.text: Hamming’s Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes is the selected published milestone.

sources.title: Hamming: Error Detecting and Error Correcting Codes (1950)

events.label: 1684 · Newton/Leibniz wider development
events.text: Leibniz’s printed differential-calculus work is the selected anchor; Newton’s work and notation are separate parts of the history.

events.label: 1686 · later integral theories follow
events.text: This is the early-calculus publication anchor, not a claim that all integrals date from Leibniz’s paper. Riemann and Lebesgue milestones are later.
D’Alembert’s vibrating-string work is a dated differential-equation example. Ordinary differential equations arose through wider calculus work.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Mathematics: ordinary differential equations

events.text: Green’s mathematical-analysis essay is a dated landmark in the history of integral field theorems.
D’Alembert publishes his vibrating-string analysis containing the wave equation; the full subject develops much later.
Lorenz publishes Deterministic nonperiodic flow. Poincaré and other earlier dynamical work remains acknowledged.

events.label: 1914 · ideal-theory landmark: 1921
events.text: Fraenkel’s abstract-ring paper is a publication milestone. The card can be read without treating ring theory as beginning there.

sources.title: From Numbers to Rings: The Early History of Ring Theory

events.label: 1832 · Galois manuscript; published 1846
events.text: Galois’s manuscript is dated before his death; Liouville’s 1846 publication is a separate dissemination milestone.
Euler publishes his Königsberg bridge problem analysis.

sources.title: Euler: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis (1736; Stony Brook translation of the original paper)

events.text: Kirchhoff’s circuit-paper tree ideas and Cayley’s tree terminology are linked but distinct nineteenth-century milestones.

sources.title: Kirchhoff (1847) — original paper on circuit equations

events.text: Dantzig develops linear programming and proposes the simplex method.

sources.title: Dantzig and the simplex method — INFORMS

events.text: Cauchy’s rigorous calculus work is a publication anchor for the later theory of complex analysis, not the end of the story.

events.label: 1960 · after classical algebraic geometry
events.text: Grothendieck and Dieudonné publish EGA I. This modern language does not erase earlier classical algebraic geometry.

sources.title: Grothendieck & Dieudonné: Éléments de géométrie algébrique I (1960)
The Stacks Project: open algebraic-geometry reference

events.text: Grothendieck’s categorical geometry and Lawvere’s categorical-logic programme converge in the development of topos theory. It is a range, not a single-person invention.

sources.title: Mac Lane & Moerdijk: Sheaves in Geometry and Logic (Springer)

events.label: 1971 · Cook; Levin independently
events.text: Cook’s theorem is a landmark in computational-complexity theory; Levin’s independent formulation is also included.

sources.title: Cook: The Complexity of Theorem-Proving Procedures (1971)
P versus NP problem — Clay Mathematics Institute

events.text: RSA is published by Rivest, Shamir and Adleman. Cryptography itself and earlier public-key research are older.

sources.title: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman (1978) — original paper

events.text: Shor’s algorithm is a milestone for quantum information and computational complexity; not a completed large-scale quantum computer.

sources.title: Shor: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms
